title: True vs false Fermi surfaces in the Pseudogap regime and their transformation with doping and temperature in the Hubbard Model
abstract: Exact diagrammatic quantum Monte Carlo (DiagMC) results for the nearest-neighbor Hubbard model motivate a closer study of the pseudogap. Using the improved two-particle self-consistent approach (TPSC+), we analyze Energy (EDC) and Momentum Distribution Curves (MDC) simultaneously. We show that Fermi-liquid terminology breaks down in the pseudogap regime, requiring a distinction between true and false Fermi surfaces and zero-energy quasiparticle (ZEQ) lines. A false Fermi surface has a momentum-space spectral maximum but a frequency-space depression at zero energy, while a false ZEQ line violates the standard quasiparticle condition $\partial Σ'(\mathbf{k},ω)/\partial ω|_{ω=0}<0$.The pseudogap is driven by critical thermal spin fluctuations, which occur in two dimensions because of the Mermin-Wagner theorem. Commensurate fluctuations first open an antinodal pseudogap, leaving true Fermi arcs. With decreasing temperature, the Fermi surface evolves into hole- and electron-like false Fermi surfaces. Incommensurate fluctuations generate hot spots near the diagonal, where the pseudogap persists to the quantum critical point (QCP), whereas at $\mathbf{k}_{AN}$ it disappears before the QCP doping. There, the spectrum has two precursor antiferromagnetic (AFM) bands, both in the unoccupied ($ω>0$) region. We benchmark TPSC+ against DiagMC results for the Matsubara spectral proxy $-\mathrm{Im}[\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{k},iπT)]/π$. TPSC+ underestimates pseudogap suppression in the strong-interaction regime, reproducing DiagMC behavior at lower temperatures or doping. This proxy is equivalent to the spectral function with thermal broadening $η=πT$, which obscures features when $πT$ is not the smallest energy scale. Using $A(\mathbf{k},0)$, we find that hole-like Fermi surfaces emerge at any interaction strength at low temperature, even at weak coupling.
summary: This theoretical work investigates the complex pseudogap phase in the Hubbard model, arguing that Fermi liquid theory fails in this regime. Using advanced many-body techniques, the authors distinguish between true and false Fermi surfaces, showing that the pseudogap physics is fundamentally driven by critical thermal spin fluctuations rather than simple band structure effects.
main_problem: The paper aims to clarify the physics of the pseudogap regime in the Hubbard model, specifically distinguishing between true and false Fermi surfaces and zero-energy quasiparticle lines.
main_result: The standard Fermi liquid description breaks down in the pseudogap regime, and the emergence of false Fermi surfaces is linked to critical thermal spin fluctuations, which are better captured by real-frequency spectral analysis.
method: The study employs the improved Two-Particle Self-Consistent Approach (TPSC+) to simultaneously analyze Energy Distribution Curves (EDC) and Momentum Distribution Curves (MDC), comparing results against Diagrammatic Quantum Monte Carlo (DiagMC) data.
model_or_system: The system analyzed is the nearest-neighbor Hubbard model on a two-dimensional square lattice, described by a Hamiltonian involving hopping and on-site Coulomb repulsion.
key_observables: Energy Distribution Curves (EDC), Momentum Distribution Curves (MDC), spectral function A(k, omega) at zero real frequency A(k, 0), and the quasiparticle condition $\partial\Sigma'(k, \omega)/\partial\omega|_{\omega=0}<0$.
important_parameters: Doping ($\delta$), Temperature ($T$), and Interaction Strength ($U$). The analysis focuses on the pseudogap regime driven by spin fluctuations.
main_assumptions: The TPSC+ approach is used, which is an improvement over standard TPSC, and the analysis relies on the distinction between real-frequency and Matsubara-frequency spectral representations.
figures_summary: The notes do not provide a summary of figures, but they detail the analysis of EDC and MDC across different doping and temperature regimes.
paper_structure: The paper develops its argument by first establishing the breakdown of Fermi liquid theory, then analyzing the spectral signatures (false vs. true FS) arising from commensurate and incommensurate spin fluctuations, and finally benchmarking the TPSC+ method against DiagMC results.
why_interesting: The detailed analysis of spectral function crossovers and the failure of standard quasiparticle assumptions in the pseudogap state provides a rigorous theoretical framework relevant to understanding strongly correlated quantum materials.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. EDC curves along the diagonal (left panel) and edge (0, 0)–(π, 0) (right panel) of the BZ. The parameters are U = 6, δ = 0.12, T = 0.025. The correlation length ξ = 130. At this tem- perature, the EDC curves in both directions clearly exhibit a pseu- dogap. As momentum approaches the Fermi surface in the diagonal direction, the quasiparticle peak first moves toward zero energy, then stops at a finite energy and reverses direction. This is a characteristic signature of the precursor to the lower SDW band in this direction. For the EDC curves along the (0, 0)–(π, 0) direction, the peak posi- tion remains at negative energy even when it reaches the end of the BZ at (π, 0).

FIG. 2. Evolution of the MDC heatmaps with decreasing temper- ature. The parameters U and δ are the same as in the EDC panel Fig. 1. The lowest temperature T = 0.025 is the same as in Fig. 1. At the temperature TRC < T = 0.25 ≪W, the maximum inten- sity of the spectral function A(k, 0) is along the non-interacting FS (white line). As temperature drops to T = 0.05 < TRC, the inten- sity of A(k, 0) drops in the direction (0, 0)–(π, 0), indicating a PG in this direction. At the even lower temperature T = 0.025 < TD, the intensity of the spectral function drops around the diagonal direc- tion (0, 0)–(π, π) as well, indicating a PG in this direction as well. FIG. 3. Heat map of the imaginary part of the self-energy at zero frequency Σ′′(k, 0) obtained using TPSC+. The parameters are U = 6, T = 0.06, δ = 0.087. ξ = 42.5. The white line shows the non-interacting Fermi surface. The shadow Fermi surface Eq. (22) is a mirror image of the non-interacting FS relative to the line (π, 0) −(0, π) for this model. The imaginary part of the self- energy Σ′′(k, 0) shows a quasi-singularity along the shadow FS with maximum intensity close to the antinodal Van Hove point (π, 0).

FIG. 4. Heat map of the imaginary part of the self-energy at zero fre- quency Σ′′(k, 0) in the case of strongly incommensurate spin fluctu- ations. The parameters are U = 6, T = 0.015, δ = 0.17. ξ = 130. The white line shows the non-interacting Fermi surface. There are four shadow Fermi surfaces that are driven by four peaks in the in- commensurate spin susceptibility χsp(q, 0). Two of these shadow FS cross the non-interacting FS, creating hot spots close to the di- agonal. As a result, the pseudogap in the strongly incommensurate case forms close to the nodal direction, rather than at the antinode as in the commensurate case.

FIG. 6. The power-law scaling χsp(qmax, 0)(T) ∼T −α at the QCP, defined with the simplified criteria described in the main text. For U = 3.5, δQCP ≈0.15 and for U = 6, δQCP ≈0.2. For both interaction strengths U = 3.5 and U = 6, the coefficient of determination R2 is very high, indicating a very good fit. The power exponent α increases with U.
